analysis.one_liner: Eliminates the federal tax on large inheritances and taxable gifts.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate and gift taxes never got a vote: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in February 1999 and sat there until the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strike the estate tax, gift tax, and generation-skipping transfer tax out of the tax code, effective for deaths, gifts, and transfers after enactment [S2][S3]. These taxes apply only above large exempt amounts, so the money at stake is concentrated in the biggest estates. The bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates would gain most: the federal estate tax applies only to estates above a large exempt amount, so repeal would let the biggest inheritances pass entirely tax-free [S2]. Estates and gift-givers of all sizes would also be freed from filing estate and gift tax returns [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It would repeal the estate tax, so estates above the exempt threshold would pay nothing on transfers at death [S2][S3].
It would repeal the gift tax and the tax on generation-skipping transfers, ending filing obligations for those transfers as well [S2][S3].
The repeal would take effect immediately for deaths, gifts, and transfers occurring after enactment, rather than being phased in [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If passed, the cost would fall on the federal Treasury, which would lose the revenue now collected from estates and gifts above the exempt thresholds; that burden would be borne by federal taxpayers generally through higher deficits, other taxes, or smaller spending.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would eliminate revenue the federal government currently collects from large estates and taxable gifts, a cost that would have to be made up through other taxes, deficits, or reduced spending [S2].
The benefit would be concentrated: because the estate tax only applies above large exempt amounts, the overwhelming share of the tax cut would go to the heirs of the largest estates [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give its entire benefit to a small group — heirs of the largest estates — while the whole country would bear the lost revenue through deficits or other taxes. Even its procedural simplicity is a benefit only to that group and to estate-planning professionals. Compared against the national cost, the benefit is narrow and the cost broad, which is likely why it attracted just ten sponsors and no committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the 106th Congress ended, and never got a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Mac Thornberry introduced the bill on February 3, 1999, with nine Republican cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and received no further action.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote appears anywhere in the bill's action history before the 106th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody gained from this outcome; the estate and gift taxes stayed on the books exactly as they were, and the estates that would have been freed of the tax kept paying it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody; the estate tax stayed unchanged

for.name: Mac Thornberry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes.

for.name: 9 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the repeal bill.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As the committee holding jurisdiction, took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled before Congress ended.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that held the bill and never scheduled it for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a member of the same party without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The estate tax applies only to estates above a large exempt amount, so repeal's dollars would go almost entirely to heirs of the biggest estates; the revenue would instead be collected from other taxpayers or added to deficits.

industries.industry: Estate planning attorneys and trust services
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate estate and gift tax returns and planning, removing work the industry is paid to do, while large estates would have less need for avoidance planning.
